title: The best Kixie alternatives in 2026
summary: Kixie alternatives for 2026, ranked. Artisan runs calling inside one AI outbound system, plus Orum, Nooks, Salesfinity and more.
body_markdown:
The best Kixie alternative for most teams is[Artisan](https://www.artisan.co/) , because it puts calling inside one AI-run outbound system instead of a power-dialer-plus-texting bundle. Kixie is a capable dialer for a small or midsize business (SMB), with SMS attached. If you want an AI to run the whole motion, an all-in-one wins.


Kixie pairs a power dialer with SMS and tight CRM logging, which is why smaller sales teams like living inside it. This bundle is its strength and its ceiling. Kixie dials and texts; it does not source leads, write and send email sequences, or handle replies for you. Teams that look for an alternative usually want either deeper parallel dialing or the whole outbound job run by an AI.

## How we chose


We weighted the criteria for a buyer who is deciding whether they need a better dialer or a system that runs the whole motion:


1. How much of the outbound job the tool does. A dialer improves connect rates; a full system connects calling to sourcing, email, and reply-handling.


2. Parallel-line depth and connect economics. Line count, AI answer detection, and what the actual calling costs to run.


3. Pricing transparency. Published pricing beats demo-gated quotes, and we say so.


4. Deployment fit at scale. Pooled numbers, callback routing, CRM owner mapping, and reputation monitoring that protect a large team's connect rates.


## Why do teams look for a Kixie alternative?


Two reasons dominate: Kixie tops out as a power dialer, and it only covers calling and texting.


Kixie is built for one-at-a-time power dialing with SMS attached. This suits an SMB rep who wants to click through a list and drop texts, but it is not a high-volume parallel floor, so teams that chase more connects per hour outgrow it. Reviewers who scale up tend to move toward parallel dialers that place several calls at once with AI answer detection, which multiplies live conversations in a way single-line power dialing cannot. For the wider field, see the[best autodialers](https://www.artisan.co/blog/best-autodialers) .


The second limit is scope. Kixie dials and texts and logs to your CRM, and that is the boundary. It does not find best-fit leads, write and send personalized email sequences, or qualify and answer replies. So a real outbound motion pairs Kixie with a data provider, a sequencer, and a deliverability layer, then stitches the reporting together. The dialer is fine; the stack around it is the cost.


We hear the same triggers again and again:


-


You need more connects per hour. Single-line power dialing caps how many live conversations a rep can start.


-


Calling and texting are only part of the job. Sourcing, email, and reply-handling still live in other tools.


-


Add-ons stack up. SMS volume, extra numbers, and AI features push the real per-seat cost above the headline.


None of this makes Kixie a bad tool for its lane. It simply puts the center of gravity in the wrong place for a team that wants either serious parallel volume or the whole motion run by an AI. For the wider field, see the[best outbound dialer](https://www.artisan.co/blog/best-outbound-dialer) roundup.


## The best Kixie alternatives in 2026


### 1. Artisan: Calling inside one AI-run outbound system


Artisan is the alternative for teams that want the dialer to be a step in a larger, AI-run motion rather than a standalone bundle. Calls run as steps inside Ava's multichannel sequences alongside email and social media outreach, so the same system that sources a lead and writes the message also places the call and logs the outcome. Ava parallel dials up to three lines with AI answer detection, loads live AI talking points before the call connects, transcribes live, auto-classifies outcomes, drafts the follow-up email, and can drop a voicemail with automatic area-code matching. For what reps say on those calls, see our[cold calling scripts](https://www.artisan.co/blog/cold-calling-scripts) .


The compliance and scale story is built for real teams, not only SMBs. Numbers are pooled at the org level with personal callback routing, so a lead who calls back reaches the right rep's phone. Calling-hours enforcement, do-not-call (DNC) checks, and consent-aware recording apply automatically per lead. Central admin maps CRM owners so calls log to the right rep, and per-number call ceilings plus carrier spam-reputation monitoring protect connect rates across a large team. Numbers are available in the US, Canada, the UK, Mexico, and Colombia.


The economics are the headline against Kixie. Artisan's pricing is usage-based: Ava's work runs on credits, so you pay for what she actually performs, whether that is qualifying, enriching, personalizing, or sending. Because the wider outbound motion also lives here, you replace a data tool, a sequencer, and a deliverability layer at the same time instead of paying for a dialer and then buying the tools around it. You can try Ava for free before you commit.


The line count is a real limit. Artisan parallel dials up to 3 lines, while Nooks and Orum reach 5 to 10. A team whose entire motion is maximum-volume parallel calling, and nothing else, may still want a dedicated floor. For everyone whose calling sits inside a broader outbound motion, one system beats a dialer plus a stack.


SumUp reported a $52 cost per lead with Ava and 8 to 15 positive replies per week from previously unreachable local businesses.


**Best for:** startups through enterprise that want calling as one channel in an AI-run outbound system.


**Who should pick something else:** pure call floors whose only job is maximum-volume parallel dialing at 5 to 10 lines.


**Pricing:** usage-based, with a free trial. See[artisan.co/pricing](https://www.artisan.co/pricing) .


### 2. Nooks: High-volume parallel call floor


Nooks is the alternative for teams whose problem with Kixie is line count. It parallel dials multiple lines with AI answer detection and runs a virtual salesfloor with live coaching, which makes it popular with high-volume calling teams. If you are moving from single-line power dialing to real parallel volume, Nooks is a serious option. For a direct comparison, see[Artisan vs. Nooks](https://www.artisan.co/blog/artisan-vs-nooks) .


The trade is scope and price. Nooks is calling-only, so sourcing, email, and replies live elsewhere, and its pricing is demo-gated and billed annually, with third parties reporting roughly $4,000 to $5,000/user/year. Our[dialer roundup](https://www.artisan.co/blog/the-best-ai-dialers-and-parallel-dialers) breaks down the pure-parallel options.


**Best for:** teams that are upgrading from power dialing to a high-volume parallel salesfloor.


**Who should pick something else:** teams that want calling connected to the rest of outbound, or published pricing.


**Pricing:** demo-gated, annual; reportedly roughly $4,000 to $5,000/user/year.


### 3. Orum: Enterprise parallel with global reach


Orum suits large teams whose motion really is high-volume parallel calling across borders. It parallel dials 5 to 10 lines with AI answer detection, offers international dialing on its Ascend tier, and acquired the conversation-intelligence tool Scout AI in July 2026. For a dedicated call floor at enterprise scale, Orum is an established option. For a direct comparison, see[Artisan vs. Orum](https://www.artisan.co/blog/artisan-vs-orum) .


Like Nooks, it is calling-only, and its live page is gated, with Launch reported around $250/user/month and Ascend custom-quoted. Sourcing, email, and reply-handling live in other tools, so it solves the line-count problem but not the stack problem.


**Best for:** enterprise call floors that need 5 to 10 lines and broad international coverage.


**Pricing:** gated; Launch reported ~$250/user/month, up to 5 lines; Ascend custom, up to 10 lines.


### 4. Salesfinity: Transparent parallel pricing


Salesfinity is the pick for teams that want real parallel dialing without a demo to see the price. It publishes $149 to $349/user/month for five lines, which makes it the transparent alternative in the pure-dialer tier. For a calling team that values knowing the cost up front, this openness is a real advantage over gated rivals.


Salesfinity is still a dedicated dialer, so the same boundary applies: it dials, and the rest of your outbound stack sits elsewhere. Among standalone parallel dialers, its pricing transparency stands out.


**Best for:** calling teams that want five-line parallel dialing at a published price.


**Who should pick something else:** teams that want the dialer inside a full outbound system.


**Pricing:** $149 to $349/user/month for five lines, per Salesfinity's pricing page.


### 5. Koncert: Multiple dialing modes


Koncert fits teams that want flexibility in how they dial. It offers several modes, an AI parallel dialer, a flow dialer, and an agent-assisted dialer, so reps can match a dialing style to each campaign. This range makes it adaptable across different calling motions within one tool.


Koncert is a dedicated dialing platform, so it handles calls and not the surrounding motion. Its pricing varies by dialing mode across a public per-seat ladder from $6 to $99/user/month, so the total depends on which modes a team buys.


**Best for:** teams that want to switch between parallel, flow, and agent-assisted dialing.


**Who should pick something else:** teams that want calling unified with sourcing, email, and replies.


**Pricing:** $6 to $99/user/month public ladder, varying by dialing mode.


### 6. JustCall: Calls and SMS with a workflow layer


JustCall is a close shape-match to Kixie: a cloud phone that combines calling, SMS, and automations, aimed at SMB and mid-market teams that want their telephony and texting in one place with CRM integrations. If you like Kixie's model but want a different feature mix, JustCall is the natural like-for-like swap. For a direct comparison, see[Kixie vs. JustCall](https://www.artisan.co/blog/kixie-vs-justcall-which-should-you-choose-in-2026) .


It is more communications platform than high-volume parallel floor, so teams that chase connect-rate multipliers or a full AI-run motion will still look elsewhere. Its per-seat pricing is published.


**Best for:** SMB teams that want calls, texting, and automations in one communications tool.


**Who should pick something else:** teams that need high-line parallel dialing or an AI-run full outbound motion.


**Pricing:** published per-seat pricing, per JustCall's pricing page.


### 7. Aircall: Business phone system first


Aircall is the alternative for teams that want a proper business phone system with call-center features and a deep app-integration catalog, rather than an outbound-prospecting dialer. It handles inbound and outbound telephony well and connects to a wide set of tools, which suits support-and-sales teams that need a shared phone system. For a direct comparison, see[Artisan vs. Aircall](https://www.artisan.co/blog/artisan-vs-aircall) .


As an outbound-prospecting engine it is lighter than the parallel dialers here, and it does not run sourcing, email, or replies. It is a phone system, priced per seat and published.


**Best for:** teams that want a full business phone system with strong integrations.


**Who should pick something else:** outbound teams that want parallel dialing or an AI-run motion.


**Pricing:** published per-seat pricing, per Aircall's pricing page.


## Stay with Kixie if...


Kixie is the right call for a specific profile. Keep it if:


-


You are an SMB team that wants power dialing and SMS together in one affordable tool with tight CRM logging.


-


Your volume is modest enough that single-line power dialing keeps reps busy without parallel lines.


-


You already run a settled stack for sourcing, email, and replies, and you only need the calling-and-texting piece to sit inside it.


Switching away from a tool that fits your motion to solve a problem you do not have is a waste. If Kixie's calling-and-texting bundle matches how your small team sells, it is a defensible place to stay. If you need more connects per hour or want the whole motion run by an AI, this is your signal to move.


## How a communications dialer compares to an AI BDR


The decision hinges on whether you need better telephony or the whole outbound job done. A dialer like Kixie improves how reps call and text, and does nothing beyond that. An[AI sales agent](https://www.artisan.co/ai-sales-agent) like Ava places calls as one step in a sequence that also sources a lead, writes and sends the email, and handles the reply, all in one system.


If your team mostly needs a phone and texts, Kixie or a like-for-like swap covers it. If your team runs multichannel outbound, buying a dialer means buying and stitching a stack around it. Consolidating into an[AI business development representative (BDR)](https://www.artisan.co/blog/ai-bdr) removes both the stitching and the add-on creep.


## What changed in dialers in 2026?


-


Orum acquired the conversation-intelligence tool Scout AI in July 2026, deepening its post-call analytics.


-


Spam flagging and number reputation stayed the category's number-one buyer worry, pushing demand toward tools with automatic reputation monitoring and per-number ceilings.


-


Published dialer pricing gained ground against demo-gated quotes as buyers pushed back on quote-only models.


-


Parallel dialing kept moving from a standalone category toward a channel inside broader AI-run outbound systems.


## Frequently asked questions


**What is the best alternative to Kixie?** For teams that want calling connected to the rest of outbound, Artisan is the strongest alternative, because the dialer runs inside Ava's multichannel sequences. For teams that simply need more connects per hour, Nooks or Orum add high-volume parallel dialing at 5 to 10 lines.


**What is the best enterprise alternative to Kixie?** Artisan is the pick for teams that want calling governed inside one system: pooled org-level numbers, callback routing, automatic DNC and calling-hours enforcement, CRM owner mapping, and reputation monitoring. Orum is the enterprise choice if the motion is purely maximum-volume parallel calling across many countries.


**How much does Kixie cost?** Kixie's pricing is demo-gated, and add-ons for SMS volume, extra numbers, and AI features raise the real cost. Artisan's pricing works differently: it is usage-based, so you pay for the work Ava performs rather than for a fixed seat bundle, and you can try her for free.


**Does Kixie do parallel dialing?** Kixie centers on single-line power dialing with SMS rather than high-volume parallel calling. Teams that want several simultaneous lines with AI answer detection typically move to a parallel dialer like Nooks, Orum, or Salesfinity, or to Artisan, which parallel dials up to three lines inside a full outbound system.


**How many parallel lines does Artisan support?** Artisan parallel dials up to 3 lines with AI answer detection. Nooks and Orum reach 5 to 10 lines. For a team whose whole motion is maximum-volume calling, this line-count difference matters; for teams where calling is one channel in a broader sequence, 3 lines inside one system is usually the better trade.


**Is Artisan cheaper than a dialer plus a full outbound stack?** Usually, because Artisan consolidates the dialer, sourcing, email sending, and reply-handling into one usage-based system. A Kixie-style dialer only covers calling and texting, so a data tool, a sequencer, and a deliverability layer are separate line items on top.
